title: Gene Variants Tied to Higher Pancreatic Cancer Risk in Egyptian Patients
summary: Gene Variants Tied to Higher Pancreatic Cancer Risk in Egyptian Patients Bioengineer.org
text:
Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is one of the most aggressive cancers, and a new case-control study from Menofia University in Egypt points to inherited differences in two DNA-handling genes as possible contributors to who develops the disease and who fares worst after diagnosis. The research, published in Molecular Biology Reports, examined the OGG1 rs1052133 and CYP1A1 rs1048943 polymorphisms in 80 patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma and 80 matched controls, and found that specific variants of both genes were significantly more common among the patients.
The study focused on two biological pathways that have previously been implicated in pancreatic carcinogenesis: oxidative DNA repair and carcinogen metabolism. OGG1 encodes 8-oxoguanine DNA glycosylase, an enzyme that repairs oxidative damage to DNA, while CYP1A1 is a cytochrome P450 enzyme involved in metabolizing carcinogens. text:
NHS officials are shutting growing numbers of birth centres in a “shocking” denial of a woman’s right to have a midwife rather than a doctor oversee their baby’s birth, say campaigners.
Twelve birth centres – midwife-led maternity units – have closed in England since 2019. Birth centres play a key role in ensuring that women can choose whether to have their baby at a unit in a hospital run by doctors, at one where midwives are in charge, or at home.
Six units have shut permanently since Labour came to power in July 2024. Four others have been closed “temporarily” for so long, up to six years, that childbirth groups fear they will never reopen. Two other birth centres closed because the hospitals where they were based have begun to fall apart and will remain out of action for several years until new facilities are built.

text:
Trial failures of Novartis, Novo Nordisk heart drugs leave experts guessing
CHICAGO – An experimental Novartis drug designed to treat a genetic cause of heart disease failed to reduce deaths and non-fatal heart attacks, dashing hopes for the first of several such drugs in clinical trials.
Despite a 78% reduction of the blood particle commonly known as Lp(a), a monthly dose of the Novartis drug, pelacarsen, over nearly five years had no effect in preventing a second heart attack or reducing the risk of stroke or need for emergency procedures to unblock clogged arteries in the trial of more than 8,300 patients, according to detailed results.
“Everybody in the world, me included, thought that this was going to work,” said Dr Steven Nissen of the Cleveland Clinic, who presented the results on Nov 7 at the American Heart Association (AHA) meeting in Chicago.

ai_summary: Experimental heart drugs from Novartis and Novo Nordisk failed to meet primary clinical trial goals, surprising medical experts.

Some people may think that current problems in relations between Egypt and Sudan are a natural product of diverging interests or political visions between the two countries.

This hostility was manufactured in British laboratories to amputate the common memory of the peoples of the two countries.

Israeli restrictions have meant scarce aid- and in particular, shelter materials- is entering the strip, leaving almost all of Gaza's population exposed to the elements and health risks amid rapidly deteriorating sanitation conditions.
Abu Ramdan emphasised that the razing of infrastructure by Israel as part of its onslaught on Gaza has amplified the health risks. Overcrowded displacement camps and the cold and damp conditions inside damaged tents could expose children, infants and elderly people to an elevated risk of respiratory infections.
Meanwhile, lack of clean water, busted sewage systems, and mounting waste pose the risk of water and food contamination, as well as the spread of rodents and insects.

November 7, 2026
Millions of people now use AI chatbots as a source of news to find quick answers to questions about current events.
A 2026 survey by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, which questioned more than 90,000 people worldwide, found that 10% use AI chatbots for news on a weekly basis, a figure that is significantly higher among younger audiences.

It has been over a decade since Stephanie Wheen set out to create the UK’s first play and leisure centre specifically designed for disabled children.
Over the past 10 years, she and her team have raised millions of pounds, meticulously researched how to make the centre as inclusive as possible and spent years trialling sessions with disabled children. And soon, the doors to Gympanzees will open for the first time.
“It’s been so long in the making – I try picturing it and it’s just a lot of smiley people. I expect families are going to be quite awestruck because it’s been made for them when they’re so used to there being nothing,” said Wheen.
The idea was born in 2016 out of Wheen’s work as a children’s physiotherapist in Bristol. With her sessions constantly fully booked, she tried to get the disabled children she worked with to do more physical activity in the community so they would not need to rely so heavily on her service.

text:
No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.

‘We do not want to die from the cold’: Gaza families struggle as rain floods shelters
Mansour al-Sakni, 33, watched helplessly as rainwater flooded the makeshift shelter on the roof of a building in Gaza City's al-Tuffah neighbourhood, where he lives with his wife and four children.
The family had replaced their old tarpaulins with new ones just two weeks ago. Sakni had sold two water barrels so they could buy new sheets to keep them dry and sheltered.
But when the first winter storm swept across the Gaza Strip, the canopy offered little protection.
“We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water. The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too,” Sakni told Middle East Eye.
“We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room.”

Images posted by the IAF on social media showed the aircraft landing and taking off from the runway surrounded by barren mountains in the cold desert area, where temperatures can plummet to minus 20°C.

In the countryside west of Istanbul, trucks line up to empty mixed household waste from the city of 16 million people onto a vast landscape of decomposing rubbish, where landfill gas is captured to generate electricity at a nearby plant.

Türkiye hosts COP31 in Antalya from November 9 to 20 and has made methane reduction a priority for the climate summit.

CEDAR RAPIDS, Iowa (KCRG) - Two people were killed in a head-on crash on Highway 30 in Cedar Rapids Friday afternoon. This happened after a police pursuit that began in Marshall County.
The crash happened at about 3:10 p.m. near Highway 30 and Williams Boulevard.
In a crash report, the patrol said a driver fled law enforcement in Marshall County, leading officers on a pursuit across four counties. The patrol said the suspect fired at law enforcement during the chase, striking an occupied police cruiser.
Officers made multiple unsuccessful attempts to disable the vehicle, according to the report. The patrol said the vehicle was traveling east in the westbound lanes of Highway 30 in Cedar Rapids when officers made a final attempt to stop it. The suspect vehicle then collided head-on with another car.
The report lists two Chevrolet Impalas as the vehicles involved, but does not identify which vehicle either person killed was in.
ai_summary: Two people died following a multi-county police pursuit that ended in a vehicle crash on Highway 30 in Cedar Rapids.

Pakistan and Sudan on Saturday signed an agreement on visa-free travel for official and diplomatic passport holders, according to a statement by the Ministry of Interior.

“Under the agreement, holders of Pakistani and Sudanese official and diplomatic passports will be able to enter each other’s countries without a visa,” it stated.

“This agreement marks an important milestone in bilateral relations between Pakistan and Sudan,” it added.

Exposure to a new generation of allegedly “safe” plasticizers is linked to lower birth weight and fetal development complications, which could cause serious health problems later in life, a new peer-reviewed study found.
As the health risks in exposure to common phthalate plasticizers became clear over the last few decades, industry began switching to a new type of chemical, called Dinch, that it claimed was a “high safety”, nontoxic alternative. It is widely used in soft plastic food packaging in the United States and European Union, and is found in children’s toys, medical devices, some textiles, flooring and other consumer goods.
But it may not be as safe as industry has claimed, the New York University Langone Health analysis of federal US health data suggests. There is a dearth of research into Dinch health risks, though what exists points toward the chemicals being hormone disruptors that can impact kids’ development.
The new paper is the first to link Dinch to lower birth weight

text:
Semnan: a natural treasure trove of plant and animal diversity
TEHRAN – Semnan Province in north-central Iran is home to a remarkable diversity of plant and animal species, supported by a wide range of natural habitats stretching from forests and mountains to wetlands and vast desert landscapes.
Although often characterized as a land of desert and wilderness, the province's climatic and natural diversity has made it a valuable reservoir of botanical and faunal biodiversity.
Semnan is home to 254 bird species, 69 reptile species, 67 mammal species, 10 fish species, and four amphibian species.
One of Semnan’s most remarkable ecological features is that it is home to all eight species of felids found in Iran: the Asiatic cheetah, Persian leopard, Eurasian lynx, caracal, jungle cat, Pallas’s cat, sand cat, and wildcat.

LONDON, November 7. /TASS/. European governments are increasingly cutting pension spending, risking the loss of support from older voters, The Daily Telegraph reported.
The newspaper noted that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had proposed changing the annual pension indexation mechanism from 2030 by removing wage growth from the formula. Such measures could cost British pensioners £1,600 ($2,100) annually over the next 20 years.
Under pressure from the European Union to reduce its budget deficit, the Romanian government decided to freeze state pensions for two years starting in 2025. The newspaper added that French authorities had proposed limiting pension indexation to payments of up to €1,260 per month.

title: Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability
summary: France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?
text:
Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability
November 7, 2026
Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.
If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.
France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.
Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

ai_summary: France faces economic instability due to high public debt and political gridlock, contrasting sharply with Germany's more stable fiscal outlook.

text:
Novaya Gazeta – Russia’s most prominent independent newspaper – is being shut down. On 29 October, two things became known: Novaya was being evicted from its newsroom, and banks would stop processing readers’ donations to Novaya (its only legal income). Insiders spoke of the risk of Novaya being declared an extremist organisation – then any employee could be jailed: a journalist, an editor, an accountant, a cleaner. Closing was safer.
Novaya Gazeta is a second family to me and to many journalists now scattered around the Earth. For me it is my first family, too – my adopted sister also worked at Novaya, and it’s funny how alike we turned out.
I bought Novaya for the first time when I was 14. I opened it to an article by Anna Politkovskaya about the “cleansing” of the Chechen village of Mesker-Yurt by Russian soldiers. People stopped for minor traffic violations will no longer be referred to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
The mayor of Houston, the most populous city in the US state of Texas, has ordered the city’s police force to sharply limit its cooperation with the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
John Whitmire’s executive order came on Friday, days after Democrats swept statewide offices in the traditionally Republican state.

title: SPECIAL REPORT: Inside Lagos communities where public drains have become sewage channels
summary: PREMIUM TIMES visited several communities on Lagos Island and found residential buildings discharging wastewater and sewage into public drains, exposing residents to health risks despite environmental laws prohibiting the practice. The post SPECIAL REPORT: Inside Lagos communities where public drains have become sewage channels appeared first on Premium Times Nigeria .
text:
Just after dawn on a humid morning in May, Enomfon Okure stepped out of her apartment on Braimoh-Igbo Street in Itafaji, Lagos Island, preparing for another workday in nearby Ikoyi.
Before taking a few steps, she instinctively covered her nose.
The stench had become part of her mornings since January 2025, when she moved into the neighbourhood with her family.
Beside the road, black wastewater flowed slowly through an open drainage channel. At intervals, more toilet waste gushed from pipes protruding from nearby buildings and emptied directly into the drain.
Flies hovered over the murky water as pedestrians squeezed along the narrow walkway, trying to avoid contact with it.
For Mrs Okure, a nurse and mother of four, the scene has become an inescapable part of daily life.
“I am struggling to survive here,” she told PREMIUM TIMES.

Russia says it hit targets in and around Kyiv in massive overnight strike
Nov 7 - Russia said its forces carried out a massive overnight strike on what it described as targets in Ukraine's military-industrial sector and energy and transport infrastructure in Kyiv and the surrounding region.
In Kyiv, Russia's defence ministry said strikes hit the Northern Bridge — which it said was being used to transport weapons, military equipment and vehicles for the Ukrainian armed forces — and the Meridian plant, which Russia says produces Flamingo cruise missiles.
The ministry also said the strikes damaged several energy and industrial facilities in the Kyiv region, including a power plant, an electricity substation and a munitions manufacturing facility.
It added that Russian forces struck an electricity substation in the Zhytomyr region and a cargo vessel in the Black Sea that it said was transporting military equipment and dual-use goods to Ukraine. REUTERS

Antibiotics have transformed modern medicine, making once-deadly infections treatable. But as bacteria become increasingly resistant to the drugs designed to kill them, that progress is under threat.
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is responsible for an estimated 35,000 deaths each year in the European Union, with its health impact comparable to that of influenza, tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS combined.
"Antibiotic resistance is when bugs can't get treated with the medicines anymore that we usually use to treat them," Fiona Walsh, a professor at Maynooth University in Ireland, told Euronews. Her research focuses on resistance across human, animal and environmental health.

title: Do not investigate Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office
summary: The US presidential pardon power has created a constitutional absurdity that can protect those accused of corruption.
text:
Do not investigate Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office
The United States’ presidential pardon power has created a constitutional absurdity in which exposing corruption may protect those responsible.
In a functioning constitutional democracy, allegations of corporate corruption would ordinarily invite immediate investigation. Congress would demand documents, summon executives and expose wrongdoing to public scrutiny.
With Democrats having won control of both houses of Congress, the expectation will be that they exercise these oversight powers vigorously. In Donald Trump’s America, however, there is a compelling argument for doing precisely the opposite.
If the objective is criminal accountability rather than political theatre, the incoming Democratic majorities might be better advised to preserve the evidence but postpone public congressional investigations and disclosures concerning potential criminal wrongdoing by Trump’s corporate allies until he leaves office in January
ai_summary: The author argues that incoming Democratic majorities in Congress should delay investigations into Trump's corporate allies until he leaves office to ensure criminal accountability.

Artem Lytvyn was crossing a field when the bang happened. Up ahead was a tree line. Not far beyond that the Russian border. The 25-year-old Ukrainian soldier had spent five days trekking to a dangerous forward position in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. Along the way he and six comrades dodged drones, and killed two Russians in a foxhole.
A few hundred metres short of his destination, he trod on a mine. “I didn’t hear anything. It was a magnet type. My rifle set it off,” Lytvyn said. He applied two tourniquets to his shattered right leg and pulled off his combat boot. Fellow soldiers dragged him and another wounded platoon member, Siava, into bushes. The same blast ripped off Siava’s leg. He died two days later.

THE preoccupation of exchange rate fundamentalists in Pakistan with a single, partial indicator — Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) — is astonishing. As Nadeem ul Haque argued in an illuminating article, fixing or deliberately boosting exchange rates effectively ended with Bretton Woods’ collapse in the 1970s. Research has since confirmed that the exchange rate is a market price — the price of one currency in terms of another, determined by underlying economic conditions — and not a policy tool.
Hence, the exchange rate is an endogenous variable reflecting domestic inflation, productivity, external balances, capital flows, reserve adequacy, fiscal credibility, interest-rate differentials, and market expectations. As Haque notes, “The rupee does not weaken because someone decides to weaken it. It weakens because underlying conditions make the existing price unsustainable.”

text:
The government has selected 28 priority products and technologies, including semiconductors and artificial intelligence, for public and private investments totaling over ¥370 trillion, which are a pillar of its growth strategy, sources said Friday.
The list was presented at the day’s meeting of the Council for Japan’s Growth Strategy, chaired by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
“Large-scale and strategic investment support measures are essential for establishing a domestic semiconductor supply chain,” Takaichi said at the meeting.
The 28 priority items were picked from 62 products and technologies in 17 strategic fields. They are expected to have significant economic spillover effects.

title: BOJ’s Ueda says unclear how long 2% inflation rate will remain
summary: Gov. Kazuo Ueda indicated an awareness that the goal had been reached hasn't yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public.
text:
Bank of Japan Gov. Kazuo Ueda said that while his nation’s inflation rate has reached policymakers’ target, it’s unclear how long it will stay there, and indicated it hasn’t yet become embedded among the broader Japanese public.
“Underlying inflation is 2% — our goal is to keep it there,” Ueda said in a question and answer session after delivering a speech at the International Monetary Fund in Washington on Friday. “I think we are in equilibrium,” he said. “Whether we could stay in that equilibrium for a very long time to come, we still don’t know.”
The remarks come a week after the BOJ marked a milestone by declaring that underlying inflation had reached the bank’s 2% target for the first time since the goal was introduced in 2013. Ueda didn’t offer any specific guidance on the central bank’s appetite to raise interest rates further, in an exchange with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.

PAKISTAN’S external debt has nearly doubled in a decade — from $68.7bn in 2015 to $135.1bn in 2025 — according to a new World Bank report. Public and publicly guaranteed debt accounts for $107.1bn of the total, private debt for $17.6bn, and short-term borrowing for $10.45bn.
China is the largest single creditor with $22.4bn outstanding, followed by the World Bank and Asian Development Bank. The rise itself is not surprising but the pace is striking. Much of this borrowing went towards plugging external financing gaps, propping up reserves, and repaying older loans to keep the economy running.
The debt spike describes an economy that invests, produces and earns too little to service what it owes. Debt has become the main constraint on our fiscal and economic prospects. The poems in this volume place everyday objects alongside images of brutality, starvation, and war to emphasise the absurdity of continuing one’s mundane life as the world falls apart. title: ‘Chalre Chalre Waal’: What Indians don’t hear in the Saraiki song that’s become a cross-border hit
summary: The melody resonates with a community’s identity, historical trauma and a struggle for recognition,
text:
In the early 2000s, growing up in a small village in Dera Ismail Khan in Pakistan, my childhood had a very specific sound: the whirring of an old cassette tape recorder in our home.
While my mother went about her daily chores, she would play the song Chalre Chalre Waal. Long before smartphones, algorithms or high-definition music videos existed, that traditional song played on loop, echoing through our courtyard.

text:
We’re still days away from knowing who won key midterm races in Alaska. Elections officials are planning to release more votes Monday and Tuesday as the high-profile statewide races for Congress and governor remain uncalled.
In the meantime, though, there’s plenty of data to sift through.
The Division of Elections released a large file known as the “cast vote record” early Wednesday morning with data from the roughly 204,000 ballots that have been scanned so far.
It’s an incomplete sample of the overall vote. The version released Wednesday does not include ballots from rural and remote precincts that count their Election Day votes by hand, nor does it include what’s expected to be tens of thousands of remaining early and absentee votes set to be counted next week.
That means it’s difficult to extrapolate election outcomes — newly counted votes could have a significant impact on who ultimately wins each race.
But the data, despite its limitations, has some interesting stories within it.

title: Apple’s autocomplete restrictions include ‘Dictator Trump’ and ‘Sleepy Joe,’ researcher finds
summary: The find offers insight into the tradeoff between guessing what users are trying to say and preventing the devices from offering offensive suggestions.
text:
Washington – Apple has an undisclosed multilingual gray list of tens of thousands of words and phrases that its iOS keyboard will not autocomplete or swipe-type, a researcher said on Friday.
The list is not a ban. iPhone users can still type what they like when drafting emails and texts. But the words on the list will not be suggested to users via autocomplete or swipe-typing in most cases. The researcher, Derik Kauffman, said the find opens a window into how Apple manages the tradeoff between anticipating what hundreds of millions of iPhone users are trying to say and preventing the devices from offering offensive or politically charged suggestions to users — something he said could quietly shape how they communicate.
“It’s a very light-touch form of censorship,” said Kauffman. “But at the scale that Apple is operating, it only takes a light touch to have a big impact.”

text:
Three charged after man allegedly interfered with corpse at Browns Plains funeral home
Three people have been charged after a man allegedly interfered with a corpse at a funeral home south of Brisbane.
Police say two men and a woman visited a funeral home on Eastern Road at Browns Plains at about 1pm yesterday after arranging to view the body of a man who was known to them.
"It is alleged one of the men interfered with the corpse whilst at the premises and fled the scene before police arrival," police said.
The second man and the woman were arrested at the scene, while the other man was arrested at about 6:30pm at a Browns Plains residence.
The two men, aged 47 and 38, and the 43-year-old woman were all charged with one count each of misconduct with a corpse, entering a premises with intent to commit an indictable offence, and being armed with intent to enter a premises and commit an indictable offence.
They are all due to appear in the Brisbane Magistrates Court today.

The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.

text:
Meteorologists warn that an unprecedented early disruption of the polar vortex could increase the risk of cold spells across the Northern Hemisphere, although its impact on the coming winter remains uncertain.
Meteorologists are monitoring an unusually early weakening of the polar vortex, a vast circulation of cold air above the Arctic, raising the possibility of colder weather across parts of Europe, North America and Asia in the weeks ahead.
The disruption could increase the likelihood of colder spells across northern and central Europe, including parts of Scandinavia, the British Isles, Germany and Poland.
The phenomenon normally strengthens throughout autumn, reaching its peak around January before gradually weakening towards the end of winter. Major disruptions, which can allow Arctic air to move further south, typically occur between January and March.

text:
US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions
WASHINGTON, Nov 6 (Reuters) - The US Treasury said on Friday that it had imposed financial sanctions on eight money services firms based in Canada that it alleges have facilitated transactions with sanctioned Iranian entities.
The sanctions effectively cut the firms off from the dollar-based financial system, blocking any assets that the firms may have in the United States and prohibiting any transactions with US persons or entities.
The actions are the latest in a series of Treasury moves against firms outside the United States that it says help Iran get around US sanctions, as Washington keeps up pressure on Tehran.
"Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent. “Treasury will pursue and disrupt the Iranian regime’s financial channels anywhere in the world.”

Cair shuts down Florida office as judge declines reversal of terrorist designation
The Council on American Islamic Relations (Cair) has shut down its operations in Florida after a judge declined to reverse the terrorist designation of the group that the state legislature and the governor had imposed earlier this year.
Chief Judge Allen C Winsor of the US District Court for the Northern District of Florida made his decision on Wednesday, while acknowledging Florida's “novel - and perhaps unprecedented" new law allowing for terrorist designations of non-profit groups without due process.
But ultimately, he said Cair's emergency request did not adequately prove that the group was suffering a criminal punishment.
Winsor did, however, say Florida officials cannot prevent Cair from accessing legal services. Florida officials also pledged not to prosecute Cair's board, its staff, or its third-party associates.
Cair has said it will now appeal the decision.

Around 700 of the rescued migrants are due to be transferred to Tenerife to relieve pressure on reception facilities, while several people required hospital treatment.
Spain's Maritime Rescue Service (Salvamento Marítimo) has assisted 854 migrants aboard seven small, open motorised fishing vessels in waters off the Canary Island of El Hierro since the early hours of Friday morning. The boats were escorted to the harbour of La Restinga, in the municipality of El Pinar, where those on board received medical attention.
Of those brought ashore, 350 were transferred to Tenerife on the scheduled morning ferry service. The Spanish authorities are planning to relocate a further 350 migrants on Friday afternoon's crossing to ease pressure on reception facilities on El Hierro.

The video game’s latest installment seems disillusioned with the kind of militarism it did so much to promote.
When Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare debuted in 2007, it was a revelation. Whereas earlier games in the series followed the familiar pattern of World War II stories, Modern Warfare recreated 21st century combat in groundbreaking graphic fidelity.
Players undertook nighttime counterterrorism raids, maneuvered tanks through urban environments that bore striking resemblance to Baghdad, and controlled drones through infrared displays on missions almost indistinguishable from real footage of U.S. bombing runs. Call of Duty has since become one of the most lucrative video game series in history, offering players all of the excitement of the war on terror with none of its controversy.

Pope Leo begins a 12-day, 3-country South America tour after his cancer surgery
MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV has arrived in South America for a 12-day, three-country journey that will be his longest and most far-reaching trip yet, and his first major overseas visit since undergoing lung cancer surgery.

For much of the past decade, energy debates often pitted fossil fuels against clean energy. Governments announced dates for phasing out technologies, investors tried to anticipate which industries would lose favor, and energy policy increasingly became entangled with political identity.
The war with Iran has exposed the limitations of approaching energy policy that way. When supplies are disrupted and prices rise sharply, governments become much less interested in ideological consistency and much more interested in keeping fuel available, electricity reliable, and costs manageable.
That shift is now visible across oil, natural gas, nuclear power, renewable energy, transmission, and storage. President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's term ended in May, but his government declared a "transition period" that gave him an extra year in office to prepare for the first nationwide democratic elections, which are due in April and May 2027.

Paraguay has enjoyed relative stability following its transition to democracy in the early 1990s. However, the nation is the region’s largest producer of marijuana and traffics more illegal cigarettes than any country in the Western Hemisphere. Organized crime in Paraguay benefits from rampant, widespread corruption, and criminal opportunities come from being wedged between South America’s two largest drug consumers in Brazil and Argentina, and being adjacent to one of the region’s burgeoning narcotics hubs in Bolivia.
While Paraguay does not suffer high homicide rates, it is a major route for the trafficking of drugs and firearms. In addition to local criminal organizations, foreign crime networks — especially Brazil’s PCC — also operate in Paraguay, and a small but persistent guerrilla group has added to the nation’s security challenges.

A public opinion poll is a snapshot of a moment; a wipe-out election such as Tuesday’s midterms has roots that run deeper into history.
The word “historic” is thrown around so much these days; it has been shorn of meaning. But make no mistake, what happened this week is historic. There has not been a governing party wipe-out on this scale in the US since the 1974 midterms – also known as the “Watergate election”. That’s more than half a century ago.

GOP 'Got Mauled' After Redistricting Push
President Trump's big bet on redrawing House maps to lock in a Republican edge instead helped Democrats reclaim the chamber. His push prodded at least eight GOP-led states into mid-decade redistricting designed to squeeze out as many as 16 Democratic seats, but not a single targeted Democratic incumbent lost on Tuesday, the Hill reports. Instead, new lines fractured conservative strongholds and forced Republican incumbents into unfamiliar territory in places like Texas, North Carolina, and Ohio. Democrats flipped multiple Republican seats, including districts Trump easily carried in 2024.
The Republican redistricting push "simply did not anticipate" an electorate that swung toward House Democrats by around 13 points, the New York Times reports. summary: BERLIN, Nov 6 - Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) have agreed to back Ilse Aigner from the Bavarian Christian Social Union for the office of German president, German media said on Friday, after weeks of tension between the two sister parties.
text:
Merz's party backs former minister Ilse Aigner for German president, media reports say
BERLIN, Nov 6 - Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) have agreed to back Ilse Aigner from the Bavarian Christian Social Union for the office of German president, German media said on Friday, after weeks of tension between the two sister parties.
Aigner, currently speaker of the Bavarian state parliament, would become Germany's first female head of state if she is elected by the Federal Convention, made up of the lower house of parliament, or Bundestag, and representatives from the 16 federal states.
Germany's president holds a largely ceremonial position, signing legislation into law and formally appointing ministers, but can play a significant role beyond daily politics as a moral voice.
A CDU spokesperson declined to comment ahead of an official announcement expected following meetings on Monday to propose a successor to President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, whose term ends next year.
ai_summary: The German CDU party has agreed to support Ilse Aigner as their candidate for the upcoming presidential election.

A king who ruled at Egypt’s peak
Amenhotep III ascended the throne as a teenager and ruled for nearly 38 years, from around 1390 to 1350 BCE, during the height of the 18th Dynasty. His reign left behind temples, palaces and statues that historians still study today, among them the Colossi of Memnon near Luxor, a pair of towering stone figures that once guarded his mortuary temple.

For more than half a century, Norway’s oil and gas production has been underpinned by a handful of very large discoveries, the last of which, Wisting in the Barents Sea, was made more than a decade ago. Since then, exploration on the Norwegian Continental Shelf (NCS) has increasingly focused on smaller finds close to existing infrastructure, allowing operators to bring new volumes online faster and at lower cost. While this approach has helped sustain production in the near term, it will not be enough to arrest the NCS’s projected decline through to 2040. Rystad Energy's base-case outlook indicates that production will fall short by 1.9 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd) by 2040, highlighting the scale of the challenge facing the country's upstream sector.

Taiwan says it is closing its representative office in Papua New Guinea and will stop buying liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the country, blaming Chinese political pressure on the South Pacific nation.
Taiwan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Friday that Papua New Guinea had repeated previous demands that staff leave its office in the capital, Port Moresby, within a set deadline and had pushed for its closure.
These actions “reflect China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in other countries’ diplomatic decisions and suppress Taiwan’s international space”, it said in a statement.

title: Myanmar to conduct byelections next April
summary: The move indicates the military's increasing confidence in its ability to control territory in the Southeast Asian nation after it claimed advances following a string of offensives
text:
Myanmar will hold byelections next April, the polling commission said on Friday (November 6, 2026), encompassing areas where the pro-military parliament could not previously hold voting due to the country's devastating civil war.
The move indicates the military's increasing confidence in its ability to control territory in the Southeast Asian nation after it claimed advances following a string of offensives.
Myanmar has been embroiled in civil war since the military ousted the elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.
The junta staged phased elections last December and January, which it touted as a return to democracy following the coup.
But the highly restrictive poll was blocked in areas where rebels seized control in opposition to military rule, rejecting the elections as a charade.

text:
Re your report (Fashion and tradition: how John Smedley is innovating in a tough market, 1 November), I was fortunate to grow up with a mum who was interested in good quality clothes and fashion, and who, when I was 17, bought me a black rollneck top. Think Roger Moore. Think Illya Kuryakin (The Man from U.N.C.L.E.). Think of me in the lower sixth at a rural grammar school in Wiltshire, who missed going to the Bath blues festival at Shepton Mallet in 1970. I also missed the Isle of Wight ferry once.
I recall going on a school trip to see the film Kanał by the Polish director Andrzej Wajda. There were girls on the coach from the girls’ high school. Shock horror. What should I wear? My black polo top, of course. It would be perfect with my tweed sports jacket. And then Mum uttered those immortal words: “It’s made by John Smedley. You can wear it with anything.”
She was right. She had good taste and she wanted me to have good taste. So thanks, Mum, and thanks John Smedley (and Bill Nighy)

title: Two tankers strike mines in Strait of Hormuz: IRGC Navy
summary: TEHRAN – The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy says two oil tankers attempting to navigate unauthorized routes through the Strait of Hormuz struck mines and caught fire.
text:
Two tankers strike mines in Strait of Hormuz: IRGC Navy
TEHRAN – The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy says two oil tankers attempting to navigate unauthorized routes through the Strait of Hormuz struck mines and caught fire.
In a statement on Friday, the force said one tanker was struck in the eastern part of the strait and the other inside the waterway. Both vessels had switched off their navigation and identification systems and were attempting to exit through prohibited routes with the backing of what the IRGC described as the “aggressor and terrorist US military.”
The IRGC Navy said the vessels were halted after the explosions, adding that the strait would remain closed until Iran’s seven conditions were met.
It warned that US Central Command (CENTCOM) efforts to direct tankers through unauthorized, mine-contaminated routes would result in repeated failures.
ai_summary: The Iranian IRGC Navy claims two oil tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz after attempting to use unauthorized routes.

A Peel P50, officially recognised as the world's smallest production car, is expected to fetch as much as £60,000 at auction.
Iconic Auctioneers, of Ashorne, Warwickshire, has put an estimate of £40,000 to £60,000 on the microcar, which goes under the hammer on 14 November.
The three-wheeled vehicle measures just 4.5ft long and 3.5ft wide – enough room for one adult and one shopping bag.
The P50 was built by the Peel Engineering Company, which produced it on the Isle of Man in 1964.
When new, the car retailed at £199, equivalent to £3,635 today.
It was designed as a city car with a top speed of nearly 40mph.
ai_summary: A rare Peel P50, recognized as the world's smallest production car, is expected to sell for up to £60,000 at an upcoming auction.

title: European Commission creates anti-Russian sanctions office
summary: According to Commission Spokesperson Siobhan McGarry, the office will bring together the commission’s work "on the entire economic sanctions lifecycle"
text:
BRUSSELS, November 6. /TASS/. The European Commission has created its first permanent sanctions office that will work against Russia, Commission Spokesperson Siobhan McGarry said at a briefing.
"Yesterday we announced at the meeting, the high-level meeting of sanctions coordinators, the creation of this new sanctions office inside the Commission that will bring together the commission’s work on the entire economic sanctions lifecycle," she said.
"We are working on our 22nd sanctions package right now," McGarry added, without indicating the timeline for its presentation. Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

text:
Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and U.S. senator, dies at 89
Jay Rockefeller, who served as West Virginia's governor and U.S. senator and was the last member of his family's political dynasty, has died at the age of 89.
He died Thursday night at his home in Washington, said Mary Stewart, vice president for external affairs at WETA, the public broadcasting station where Rockefeller's wife, Sharon, is president and CEO.
Rockefeller, a Democrat and the scion of one of the nation's richest families, spent a half century in public service in one of the poorest states. He arrived in 1964 as a worker in an anti-poverty program, was elected governor a dozen years later. He served two terms and then spent 30 years as a U.S. senator.
"I could not imagine a more rewarding career," Rockefeller said upon his retirement in 2015.

title: Protests and reforms: France's rising debt costs threaten stability
summary: France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?
text:
Protests and reforms: France's rising debt costs threaten stability
November 6, 2026
Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.
If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.
France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.
Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook
ai_summary: France faces economic instability due to high public debt and rising costs, contrasting with Germany's more stable fiscal outlook.

text:
A British town crier has been named the world’s loudest woman after recording a shout of 105.9 decibels, Guinness World Records said.
Brenda Willison shouted “oyez” during an official attempt on September 9, earning the records for the loudest female town crier and the loudest individual female shout, UPI reported.
“Oyez”, traditionally used by town criers to attract attention, means “hear ye” and comes from Anglo-Norman or Old French.
Willison, who said she did not believe the attempt represented her loudest possible shout, became Peterborough’s town crier in 1987.
She told Guinness World Records that her daughter had entered her for the role after seeing an advertisement in a local newspaper.
Her daughter wrote that if Willison stood outside one of the two cafés she managed at a country park and shouted “chips”, she could be heard at the other, one and a half miles away.

title: 503kph on Abu Dhabi's E11: BYD electric hypercar sets astonishing speed record
text:
History was made on Sunday on a stretch of desert road in Abu Dhabi's Al Dhafra region, as a hypercar clocked a record-breaking 503.17kph.
The Yangwang U9 Xtreme broke the previous world speed record of 496.22kph, the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) announced on Friday. The same car set the previous record in Germany in September 2025.
The latest speed test took place on Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed International Road (E11) in Al Dhafra, where the company worked with authorities to close a 10km stretch of road. The trial used 7km of the route.
German racing driver Marc Basseng was behind the wheel and completed four runs over two days. According to the FIA, engineers adjusted the car on the second day to push its performance further.
Unlike the previous attempt, which took place at the ATP Papenburg automotive testing facility in Germany, the latest record was set on a public road.

title: Magnitude-6.1 quake hits off Tokyo, no tsunami alert issued
text:
Magnitude-6.1 quake hits off Tokyo, no tsunami alert issued
TOKYO: A magnitude-6.1 earthquake struck off the coast of Tokyo on Friday (Nov 6), Japanese authorities said, but no tsunami alert was issued.
The shallow quake hit at 7.39 pm (6.39pm, Singapore time) in the sea off the coast of the country's Kanto region, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said on its website.
Its epicentre was about 169km southeast of Asahi, which is just east of the capital Tokyo, according to the United States Geological Survey.
The JMA said it recorded a "seismic intensity 3" on Japan's 0-7 scale, meaning that "almost everyone indoors feels the shaking" and "dishes on shelves may rattle".
There were no immediate reports of damage or injuries.
Japan is one of the world's most seismically active countries, sitting on top of four major tectonic plates along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire".
The archipelago, home to around 125 million people, typically experiences hundreds of jolts every year
ai_summary: A magnitude-6.1 earthquake occurred off the coast of Tokyo, Japan, with no tsunami alert issued and no immediate reports of damage.

text:
If you are looking for something positive after Thursday's shocking stock beatdown, you have come to the right place ahead of the weekend.
History suggests stocks tend to do well after the extreme volatility we saw two days removed from the Election Day blue wave.
The VIX volatility index (^VVIX) — better known as Wall Street's fear gauge — jumped as much as 70% on Thursday. A move this large has only happened eight times since 1991, according to data from CBOE.
Here's what happened to the S&P 500 on average after the eight prior extreme moves:
- 1 month later: +3.0% (7 of 8 times positive)
- 3 months later: +7.1% (6 of 8 times positive)
- 6 months later: +10.4% (8 of 8 times positive)
- 1 year later: +14.7% (7 of 8 times positive)
While somewhat comforting, it doesn't exactly erase from the minds what happened in the markets yesterday, as risk was repriced for a Democratic control of the House and Senate.

title: Lions rally past Wiz to take Korean Series lead
summary: DAEGU, Nov. 6 (Yonhap) -- The Samsung Lions came from behind to defeat the KT Wi...
text:
Lions rally past Wiz to take Korean Series lead
By Yoo Jee-ho
DAEGU, Nov. 6 (Yonhap) -- The Samsung Lions came from behind to defeat the KT Wiz 5-1 in Game 3 of the Korean Series at home Friday, taking a lead in the best-of-seven showdown by riding one big inning.
 Starter Ariel Jurado tossed seven innings of one-run ball and captain Koo Ja-wook delivered a two-run triple in the crucial second inning before a sellout crowd of 23,550 at Daegu Samsung Lions Park in the southeastern city of Daegu. The Lions now lead the series 2-1, with Game 4 scheduled for 2 p.m. Saturday in Daegu.
Park Seung-kyu smoked a solo shot for some insurance in the eighth.
This is the 18th Korean Series in which teams were tied at 1-1 through two games. In those instances, Game 3 winners went on to capture the title 16 times.
 The Lions prevailed despite being outhit 7-4.
 jeeho@yna.co.kr
(END)

summary: [Capital FM] Nairobi -- Rwanda has launched Africa's first clinical trial of a long-acting injectable drug for malaria prevention, marking a potential shift in how the disease is prevented as drug resistance and climate change threaten progress against the mosquito-borne illness.
text:
Nairobi — Rwanda has launched Africa's first clinical trial of a long-acting injectable drug for malaria prevention, marking a potential shift in how the disease is prevented as drug resistance and climate change threaten progress against the mosquito-borne illness.
The Phase 1b trial, launched by Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV) in partnership with Rwandan health research organisation Rinda Ubuzima, will assess the safety and tolerability of MMV371, an experimental drug designed to provide extended protection against malaria through a single injection.
The injectable could potentially protect recipients for an entire malaria season, reducing the need for frequent preventive medication if its safety and effectiveness are established.
The trial marks the first Phase 1 study of a malaria-prevention long-acting injectable to be conducted in Africa and will involve adults and adolescents in Rwanda.

TOKYO – A 6.1-magnitude earthquake struck off the coast of Tokyo on Nov 6, the Japanese authorities said, but no tsunami alert was issued.
The shallow quake hit at 7.39pm local time in the sea off the coast of the country’s Kanto region, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said on its website.
Its epicentre was about 169km south-east of Asahi, which is just east of the capital Tokyo, according to the United States Geological Survey.
The JMA said it recorded a “seismic intensity 3” on Japan’s 0-7 scale, meaning that “almost everyone indoors feels the shaking” and “dishes on shelves may rattle”.
There were no immediate reports of damage or injuries.

ROME, November 6. /TASS/. The benchmark index for global food prices saw a slight decline in October, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations’ (FAO) latest Food Price Index.
The FAO Food Price Index (FFPI), which measures the monthly change in international prices of a basket of food commodities, averaged 133.9 points in October 2026, down 1.6 points (1.2 percent) from its revised September level. Price indices for cereals, dairy and meat products decreased from the previous month, while the vegetable oil price index increased only marginally and the sugar price index rose markedly. As the organization noted, the decline occurred against a backdrop of subdued demand.
Despite a decline in October, the FFPI is 5.9% higher than it was a year ago, yet it remains 16.4% below its peak from March 2022.
In September, the FAO recorded its highest price level since November 2022 amid logistical challenges and drought in several regions.

title: Could CRISPR cure rare diseases before birth? Scientists are getting closer
summary: Researchers are exploring fetal gene editing to treat rare genetic disorders before they cause lasting damage.
text:
One of the keys to curing a rare disease is treating patients early. But what if you treated them before they were born?
Over the past decade, several researchers have pursued this provocative idea. Now, they are starting to make meaningful progress in fetal gene editing, an approach that holds the potential to stop genetic disorders before it's too late.
"If you really want to prevent the worst ravages of the disease, you can't wait until they're born," said Kiran Musunuru, a gene editing expert at the University of Pennsylvania. "You've got to go in utero."
The futuristic technique is benefiting from new advances in prenatal diagnostics and CRISPR, the Nobel Prize-winning DNA editing tool. Other scientists pursuing the idea include David Stitelman at the Yale School of Medicine, Tippi MacKenzie at University of California, San Francisco, and Aijun Wang, a biomedical engineer at UC Davis.

Filed on Monday 2 November in a court in the US state of California, the lawsuit is believed to be the first to accuse Google of negligence over AI-powered search features accessed through a school-issued Chromebook, one of the company's low-cost laptops widely used in schools.
The girl, identified as Emma, was unable to access Google's Gemini app or OpenAI's ChatGPT, as both had been blocked by her school. However, she could still access Google's search engine, which includes AI-powered features.

title: ‘Dilwali Diwali’ review: For once, a film is too short to realise its ambitions
summary: Ritesh Menon’s Hindi film is out on Netflix.
text:
Dilwali Diwali rests on a solid idea. A striving engineer who lives in Norway buys an apartment in a posh complex for his family in Mumbai, but they prefer the house in which they grew up. They sneak back to their home whenever they can and hotfoot it to the new dwelling when the son appears on a video call.
The son, Ansh (Mihir Ahuja), declares that he will be visiting for Diwali, throwing his father Sudhir (Manoj Pahwa) and mother Sukhmani (Neelu Kohli) into a tizzy. Ansh arrives to find parents who are behaving strangely and his sister, Mahi (Aurra Bhatnagar) wrapped up in her own world.
Ritesh Menon’s Dilwali Diwali, which is out on Netflix, reveals its shortcomings through its duration. For once, the complaint is that a film is too short – it runs for a mere 61 minutes .
The truncated length doesn’t do justice to the themes of Ritu Mago’s screenplay: gentrification forced down the throats of people who prefer bustling and noisy neighbourhoods; an aspiration for higher living stand
ai_summary: A review of the film Dilwali Diwali suggests the movie's short runtime prevents it from fully exploring its themes of gentrification and family dynamics.

text:
Trees are experiencing an “early spring” because of mild UK temperatures this autumn, with experts warning this could cause long-term harm to pollinators.
Last month was warmer than average across all parts of the UK, with October marking the ninth consecutive month with above-average mean temperatures.
Chris Nichols, the head of conservation outcomes at the Woodland Trust, said the mild weather this autumn meant horse chestnut trees were flowering and showing signs of next year’s spring growth more than six months early.
During the extreme heat this summer, many trees underwent “early autumn”, where they wilted and lost their leaves prematurely. Experts said England’s ancient oak trees were dying as a result of high temperatures and drought, as trees and ecosystems struggle to adapt fast enough to the changing climate. Scientists have said the higher than average temperatures are only possible due to the climate crisis, primarily driven by the burning of fossil fuels.

An Iranian lawmaker has warned that any new US or Israeli attack could prompt missile strikes reaching Europe, adding that the response could push oil prices above $150 a barrel.
“The range of the responding missiles will also encompass Europe, and this will lead to the oil price crossing the $150 threshold,” Hosseinali Haji Deligani, a member of parliament, told Iran’s Tasnim news agency.
He said Iran’s response would be “massive, multiplied and strategic”, without geographical limits.
Haji Deligani also described the US naval blockade of Iran as “a form of war”, warning that Iranian forces would attack “at the appropriate moment”.
On Tuesday, Iran’s top military commander warned that the country’s armed forces would respond to any threat without “geographical limits”.

Authorities arrested 20 suspects after preventing the smuggling of 200,000 Captagon tablets and more than 30kg of narcotics into the country. The operation was carried out by the National Anti-Narcotics Agency in co-operation with Ras Al Khaimah Police, Iraq's General Directorate of Narcotics and Psychotropic Substances Affairs and the Federal Public Prosecution authorities.
The suspects, who are of Arab, African, and Asian nationalities, are alleged to have planned to take the drugs into the UAE through a border area in Ras Al Khaimah and distribute it in the country. The confiscated drugs included cocaine, crystal meth, marijuana and hashish, as well as the synthetic narcotic Spice.

Recent earnings from U.S. and European defense companies show conventional weapons continue to drive year-on-year growth, even alongside surging demand for advanced sensors, autonomous systems and counter-drone technology.

Geely emerged as the leading brand among imported new cars, with the Geely EX5 EM-R being the most sought-after model.

ROME, Nov 6 - For the first time since launching his far-right party this year, former army general Roberto Vannacci is showing signs of losing steam, with support slipping in the polls and activists abandoning him over internal disputes and policy disagreements.
Founded by breakaway lawmakers from the coalition League party, Futuro Nazionale (FN) has eaten into backing for Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's conservative bloc, complicating her bid to secure a second term in elections due in 2027.

A Nigerian court has disqualified Atiku Abubakar as presidential candidate for the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC), just two months before the country goes to the polls.
The Federal High Court in Abudja ruled that the leadership of the ADC, one of the three major parties contesting the January presidential election, was illegally constituted and therefore voided Abubakar's candidacy.
The party, which accused the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) of involvement in the lawsuit, says it will appeal.
Thursday's decision is "another desperate attempt to cripple the opposition and deny Nigerians the right to choose their leaders in the forthcoming general elections", ADC spokesman Bolaji Abdullahi said in a statement following the ruling.

Laura Kuenssberg has interviewed every living UK prime minister. In this special episode, she joins us to reveal how politicians attempt to control the narrative – and to diagnose the deeper dysfunction behind Britain’s political malaise.

Libyan court convicts six people for illegal drug production
TRIPOLI, Nov 6 - A court in Libya has convicted six people of producing the psychotropic substance Captagon for trafficking, the latest move to tackle the illegal spread of the amphetamine-type stimulant.
The North African nation has become a major regional transit hub for synthetic drugs and other narcotics, the UN said in January. Captagon, or fenethylline, is known as the 'poor man's cocaine' and is popular in the Middle East.
The court in Qubbah, a small town in eastern Libya, sentenced the first defendant to 25 years in prison and imposed a fine of 22,000 dinars ($3,445), the Tripoli-based attorney general office, which works for the whole country, said late on Thursday.
"The remaining defendants were convicted in absentia and sentenced to life imprisonment, with a fine of 70,000 dinars imposed upon each," the office said on Facebook.

A decline in fuel use in China’s industrial sector has led to a 3.1% decline in carbon dioxide emissions in the third quarter of the year, the Finnish climate outlet Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air has reported, as cited by Reuters.
The lower emissions from the world’s largest generator of CO2 resulted from a 4% drop in crude oil consumption, CREA said, adding that fuel use in transport dropped even more markedly, by 9% in the three-month period.
Coal consumption in China also declined in the third quarter of the year, by 3.3%, while wind and solar curtailment—or waste—fell, too. “The sharp decline in China's CO2 emissions extends a 'flat or falling' trend that began in March 2024 and has now lasted more than two years,” CREA analysts wrote.

title: Binance hack funds flow to Chinese launderers, Chainalysis says
summary: The hackers have been seen transferring stolen assets through thousands of digital wallets and across multiple blockchains to obscure their origins.
text:
Hackers behind the $6.3 billion theft from Binance Holdings are moving some of the stolen cryptocurrency through Chinese money-laundering networks, according to blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis.
The hackers, identified by U.S. authorities as members of North Korea’s TraderTraitor group, have been seen transferring stolen assets through thousands of digital wallets and across multiple blockchains in an effort to obscure their origins. North Korean hackers are said to have used Chinese money-laundering networks in previous thefts as well, and Chainalysis said that it’s tracked hundreds of thousands of dollars from the Binance theft — a fraction of the total stolen — flow into these networks.
The flows into money laundering networks, which include over-the-counter trading desks, suggest that hackers are pushing to take funds off of blockchain networks and cash them out, said Chainalysis.
ai_summary: Hackers linked to North Korea are laundering stolen Binance funds through Chinese networks to obscure their origins, according to Chainalysis.

UK house prices fell at the steepest rate in more than three years in October, marking the fourth consecutive monthly decline, as high mortgage rates hit the housing market.

Personal loans are useful for fulfilling financial needs, but wrong decisions can turn them into a source of stress. You can maintain financial stability by following these rules:
- Borrow only what you truly need: You will feel intense financial pressure if your total EMIs exceed 40% of your monthly income. You should take a loan only for critical needs like medical emergencies or education.
- Choose the best loan offer: You should compare interest rates, processing fees and terms across various banks. Use online calculators to find a plan that fits your budget.
- Pay your instalments on time: Missing an EMI results in heavy penalties and damages your credit score. You must manage your budget to set aside funds specifically for your instalments.
- Keep the tenure short: A longer tenure reduces the monthly EMI, but you pay much more in total interest. You can clear the debt faster and save money by choosing a shorter period.

Turkey halts Turkmen gas imports via Iran under US pressure
Turkey had to stop gas imports from Turkmenistan through Iran due to US pressure, Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar revealed on Thursday during a briefing with journalists.
Ankara began receiving gas from Turkmenistan in March 2025 under a deal to supply 1.3 billion cubic metres annually using Iranian infrastructure. Turkish gas importer Botas had an import licence for the arrangement valid until 2033.
However, Ashgabat cut the flow of gas in October 2025, saying the two countries had a short-term contract and that, without an agreement on volumes or prices, it could not sell gas to Ankara.
Bayraktar said earlier this year that Ankara had planned to resume gas imports from Turkmenistan via Iran, but those plans did not materialise.
He has now revealed that the real problem was the US-Iran war, which started in February.

title: Friday briefing: ​After a week of disruption, is living with threats our new normal?
summary: In today’s newsletter: From diverted airliners to hacked ​fridges, a string of disruptive incidents has exposed the ​vulnerabilities of modern ​life. ​There is now an increasingly blurred space between peace and conflict, the grey zone. Good morning. A multiplicity of hoax bomb threats divert passenger flights across Europe. A malign cyber-attack targets supermarket fridges in Belgium, Sweden, the UK and – in a sickening escalation – the cold storage facilities of France’s national blood service
text:
Good morning. A multiplicity of hoax bomb threats divert passenger flights across Europe. A malign cyber-attack targets supermarket fridges in Belgium, Sweden, the UK and – in a sickening escalation – the cold storage facilities of France’s national blood service.
The actors behind this week of chaos and disruption, be they hostile states or criminal gangs – or even enterprising teenagers – are yet to be identified. But what is certain is that they operate in a context of deepening global conflicts, building national threat and an accompanying, pervasive sense of vulnerability.
Welcome to the grey zone – that ambiguous space between routine peace and conventional military conflict, where proxies duck state accountability and cyber-tactics are developing at an alarming rate.

The ongoing dispute between China and Japan began following Takaichi’s remarks in parliament on Nov. 7, 2025, that the Self-Defense Forces could be deployed under the right to collective self-defense in “worst-case” scenarios, such as a Chinese naval blockade of Taiwan, which the prime minister said could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan.

The country’s foreign reserves stood at $57.4998 billion at the end of October, compared with $57.3482 billion a month earlier.
The latest increase brings the cumulative growth in reserves to around $6.05 billion since December 2025, when they stood at approximately $51.45 billion.
The continued accumulation of foreign reserves comes amid sustained foreign currency inflows, including remittances from Egyptians working abroad, tourism revenues, exports, and foreign investment.

The Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) said an El Nino -- a naturally recurring phenomenon of warming of waters in parts of the tropical Pacific Ocean -- has been forming since May and is expected to peak in December.
The latest phenomenon is forecast to develop into the strongest on record and bring warm, humid air into South Korea this winter, it said, citing record sea surface temperatures of the El Nino monitoring zone.
The moving average sea surface temperature for August to October measured 2.4 C above the long-term average, marking the highest for the period since records began in 1950, according to the KMA.

text:
Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom has flipped Forrest County, a once reliably Republican County named for Ku Klux Klan founder Nathan Bedford Forrest. 
With 97% of votes counted in Forrest County, Colom led Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith by 54%-44% as of Thursday, Nov. 5. That represents a 29-point swing toward Democrats in a county that Donald Trump carried in 2024 by a 58%-40% margin.
Colom, who currently has a narrow lead among votes counted, would be the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since 1881 during the Reconstruction era.
Nathan Bedford Forrest, a slave trader and Confederate general from Tennessee, served as the first grand wizard of the KKK during the Reconstruction era.
Forrest County includes the majority-Black city of Hattiesburg, the home of the University of Southern Mississippi. In 2020, a county-wide vote to remove a towering Confederate monument next to the Forrest County Courthouse in Hattiesburg failed in 51% to 49%

title: Energy drinks linked to heart attacks in young people
text:
High blood pressure, anxiety and chest pain are just some of the symptoms doctors are seeing in young people consuming caffeinated energy drinks, as a new study links the beverages with heart problems.
The drinks and workout supplements are disproportionately linked to serious cardiovascular events, including heart attacks, in research to be presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions on Friday.
A review of more than 28,000 adverse events reported to the US Food and Drug Administration between 2017 and 2025 showed caffeinated drinks were linked to heart problems far more often than regular beverages.
Cardiac issues were found particularly among adults aged 18 to 34, a group not usually considered at high risk of cardiovascular events.
While it is generally considered safe to drink about five cups of coffee a day (around 44mg of caffeine), some energy drinks contain three times that amount.

Could the earliest weakening of the polar vortex on record bring UK snow?
- Published
High above the Arctic, powerful winds usually circle the North Pole each winter, helping trap some of the coldest air on Earth.
But this circulation, known as the polar vortex, has weakened and shifted position in recent days.
While such disruptions can occur during winter, scientists say an event this early in November is unprecedented in modern observations.
Similar disruptions in past years have sometimes been followed by colder weather affecting parts of Europe and North America.
However, as this is happening so early in the season, there are few historical examples to compare with and it could throw current winter forecasts into even more uncertainty.
What is the polar vortex?
The polar vortex develops every autumn as temperatures fall in the Arctic.
Strong westerly winds form in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles (15-50km) above Earth's surface, locking the coldest air near the pole.

title: Japan’s nominal wages rise at fastest pace in almost 30 years
summary: Nominal wages rose 4.6% in September compared with a year earlier, marking the largest gain since 1997, the labor ministry reported Friday.
text:
Japanese workers’ nominal wages have risen at the fastest pace in almost three decades, underscoring sustained momentum in pay growth that will keep the Bank of Japan on track to hike interest rates as soon as December.

text:
Tempted by snacks before bed? Here's why - and what you can do about it
You've eaten dinner, you're comfortably full, and yet half an hour later you're raiding the kitchen cupboards. Sound familiar?
Research suggests about a third of people are snacking every night after their evening meal - for those aged 18-24, four in five are unable to resist.
Dietitian Dr Kristine Beaulieu says this spells trouble. She points to evidence showing that the more people eat within two hours of going to bed, the "greater the odds" of weight gain and obesity.
So, why are evening cravings so common? And what can you do to keep them in check?
Appetite peaks in the evening
Despite the fact we spend longer going without food when we are sleeping, research suggests our appetite naturally peaks in the evening, almost regardless of how much we have eaten earlier in the day.

Thyroid nodules are present in an estimated 50 to 70 percent of adults by age 60, which means a large share of the population starting GLP-1 therapy will already have one, discovered or not, before they ever take a first dose. That baseline prevalence is essential context for interpreting the black box warning that accompanies semaglutide and liraglutide, since it means the presence of a nodule and the presence of a genuine drug-related risk are two very different things that get conflated in casual discussion of these medications.

Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent, is trailing Democratic nominee Scott Colom in an extraordinarily tight race in normally solidly red Mississippi. Colom had 49.04% of the counted ballots, compared to 48.85% for Hyde-Smith, with an estimated more than 95% of the votes in, according to the Associated Press.
Colom's ultra-thin lead ticked up slightly late Thursday afternoon to 1,813 votes out of a total of 951,744 counted as of 6:17 p.m. ET, the AP said. Ty Pinkins, an independent candidate, had 20,007 votes, or 2.1% of the total count.

SINGAPORE: Even as the skies clear, Singapore is turning up the heat after the worst haze episode in more than a decade.
For most of its existence, the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA) has remained untested. Since it was enacted in 2014, no one has ever been prosecuted or sued under it. That may change with the conviction demonstrated by the government to act over the last few weeks.

Brothers Tjerayh and Tjeryan Coleman-Ware started cutting hair in their back shed — now they operate the first barber shop in Ceduna for five decades.
The shop doubles as the only 100 per cent Aboriginal owned and operated shop on the town's main street.
Tjerayh was 15 years old when he first started using the clippers and is trying to meet a need he experienced as a younger person.
"Just growing up with all the brothers and all that, there was no one to cut our hair, so we'd just take it in turns cutting each other's hair," he said.
"I started to enjoy it a bit more than them.
"I just like seeing someone come in and their hair might be all over the place and maybe not feeling too good about how they look and all that. And then after leaving the chair you know, they feel better about themself."

text:
Gas peakers have always had one decisive economic advantage: they were relatively cheap to build.
A peaking plant could sit idle for most of the year, then start when demand and electricity prices surged. Its fuel was expensive and its efficiency often mediocre, but low upfront costs made that acceptable. The owner did not need thousands of operating hours to recover an enormous initial investment.
Australia has now crossed an important threshold. The country’s CSIRO, working with the Australian Energy Market Operator, finds that batteries have become cheaper than gas for supplying routine peak demand. Four-hour battery systems have moved below open-cycle gas turbines on capital cost, while their operating characteristics are better suited to the short, sharp evening peaks increasingly created by abundant daytime solar.
This does not mean gas has become useless. It means batteries are taking the part of the flexibility market that gas peakers were best paid to serve.

Champion of remote education Jan Heaslip OAM dies at age 87
The founding president of the Northern Territory Isolated Children's Parents' Association and remote education advocate, Jan Heaslip OAM, has passed away, aged 87.
Ms Heaslip was also the first chair of the college council of St Philip's College in Alice Springs, helping transform the school into a full-day and boarding school.
A passionate advocate for remote education, Ms Heaslip received the Medal of the Order of Australia in 1992 for service to children's education in isolated areas.
Having arrived in Central Australia as an 18-year-old, Ms Heaslip owned and managed Bond Springs cattle station, about 20 kilometres north of Alice Springs, alongside her late husband Grant, and spent nearly seven decades in the region.
Supporter of bush kids

OpenAI has promised to set a "new standard" of listening to communities as a backlash against data centres in the US continues to grow.
On Thursday, after the Democrats had won control of Congress in the US midterm elections, OpenAI announced a National Community Compact.
"The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs and broadly shares the economic gains of AI," the compact read.
The maker of ChatGPT said that it would start to pay for its own energy on the AI infrastructure it planned to build, protect local resources, issue alerts to communities about the company's impact and publish reports in each area of the jobs OpenAI expects to create.

The Nigeria Civil Society Situation Room has expressed concern over the high cost of political campaign billboards in some states, warning that the fees could restrict opposition parties’ visibility and undermine fair competition ahead of the 2027 general elections.
The group said presidential billboard permit fees had reportedly risen to N200m in Abia State, N150m in Enugu, Kogi and Cross River, N75m in Rivers and N50m in Anambra.
It also put the reported fee in Benue State at N40m, describing the charges as a potential obstacle to candidates and political parties without substantial financial resources.
